sentences: People often confuse the tragic with misfortune, as if everything painful, disastrous, or catastrophic were tragic.
This confusion diminishes a concept that refers to something much more precise and much deeper.

The tragic, in the strong sense, does not arise from misfortune that strikes from outside, from accidents or disasters, but from a particular structure of conflict: one in which two equally legitimate demands oppose each other without either being able to yield without fault, where duty stands against duty, and where whatever choice one makes, one is guilty.
Understanding the tragic in this way is to discover a dimension of existence that simple misfortune cannot exhaust.
The great ancient tragedies provide us with a model of this.

What is tragic there is not only that the heroes suffer and die; it is that they are caught in conflicts where every outcome is guilty, where honoring one sacred demand amounts to betraying another equally sacred.

The heroine who must choose between the laws of the city and her duties to her own, between obedience to power and loyalty to blood, does not face a simple misfortune: she faces a situation where good opposes good, where whatever choice she makes, she will fail a real duty.
There lies the tragic: not in the suffering endured, but in this tearing apart where fault is inevitable, where one can only be faithful to one value by betraying another.

This tragic structure illuminates a truth that our solution-driven era tends to obscure: not all conflicts of values can be resolved, not all legitimate demands can be reconciled, and there are situations where one cannot do good without also doing harm.
We like to believe that for every dilemma there is a good answer, that a sufficiently careful examination would allow us to decide without remainder, to do good without fault.
The tragic contradicts this reassuring belief.
It asserts that certain values are irreducibly in conflict, that one cannot honor them all, and that the choice, therefore, is a tearing apart rather than a solution.
Recognizing the tragic is to renounce the illusion that every moral dilemma has an innocent outcome.
This recognition has a significance that goes beyond the tragic scene.

For life itself contains its share of the tragic, those situations where we are caught between irreconcilable duties, where we must betray one attachment to honor another, sacrifice one value to save another.

The parent who must choose between their duties to their children and those to their elderly parents; the one who must betray a friend to be faithful to justice; the one who can save one only by abandoning the other: these experience the tragic, this tearing apart where one cannot do good without also doing harm.

Life is not only made up of choices between good and evil, where the difficulty lies in wanting good; it is also made up of choices between good and good, where whatever side one takes, one fails at something.
What to do with this recognition of the tragic?
It does not lead to despair or paralysis, as if the inevitability of fault should discourage any action.
Rather, it leads to a form of lucidity and gravity.
Lucidity: not to deceive oneself about the nature of certain choices, not to pretend they are innocent when they are not, to recognize what one sacrifices in choosing.
Gravity: to measure the weight of these choices, to assume the share of fault, not to give oneself a clear conscience at little cost.

The tragic teaches us to act while recognizing that our action, in certain situations, carries an inevitable share of harm, and to bear this share without falsely absolving ourselves or burdening ourselves fruitlessly.

The tragic is therefore not misfortune, but a truth about the structure of moral existence: that there are conflicts of values that cannot be resolved, situations where duty opposes duty, where fault is inevitable.
Recognizing this is to gain a deeper wisdom than that which believes in the harmony of all values and the innocence of all good choices.

It is to understand that living as a moral being is not only to want good against evil, but also to confront, sometimes, the tearing apart where good opposes good — and to assume, with lucidity and gravity, the share of fault that then accompanies every choice.
This recognition of the tragic, far from being pessimism, may be the mark of a moral consciousness that has reached its full maturity.

sentences: It is a singular experience, distinct from that of beauty, which thinkers have named the sublime.

In the face of certain realities that surpass us — the immensity of the sea or the starry sky, the unleashed power of a storm, the dizzying height of mountains — we experience something complex and paradoxical: a mix of fear and exhilaration, a feeling of our smallness and elevation, an emotion where the displeasure of feeling crushed transforms into a strange pleasure.
This experience of the sublime, different from the gentle satisfaction provided by beauty, deserves to be analyzed, as it reveals something profound about our condition and the resources of our mind.
What distinguishes the sublime from beauty is primarily its object and the feeling it evokes.
Beauty pleases us through its harmonious, proportionate form, which aligns with our sensitivity; it calms us, satisfies us, charms us.
The sublime, on the other hand, arises from what exceeds all form, all measure, all proportion: the immense, the formless, the disproportionate, that which surpasses our ability to grasp and measure.
And the feeling it evokes is not the gentle satisfaction of beauty, but a violent, mixed emotion, where the fear of what crushes us combines with exhilaration.
The sublime does not charm; it seizes, it disturbs, it elevates even in turmoil.
How can we explain this paradox of pleasure born from what crushes us?
Thinkers have proposed a subtle analysis.

In the face of the immense, the powerful, the disproportionate, we first experience our own smallness, our powerlessness, the limits of our capacity to grasp: this is the moment of fear, of displeasure.

But in that very movement, something within us reveals itself that surpasses this smallness: our capacity to think the infinite that we cannot perceive, to conceive what exceeds our senses, to elevate ourselves by the mind above what physically crushes us.
The sublime makes us experience our sensitive smallness, but also, by contrast, the greatness of our mind, capable of thinking what surpasses it.
The pleasure of the sublime arises from this discovery: that, while we are small in the face of immensity, we carry within us something that is not measured by it, a dimension that surpasses it.
This analysis has implications that go beyond aesthetics.

For the sublime reveals a truth about our condition: that we are beings both tiny and immense, crushed by the disproportion of the world yet capable of thinking it, conceiving it, measuring ourselves against it by the mind.
We are reeds, said a thinker, the weakest of nature, easily crushed by a trifle; but we are thinking reeds, and through thought, we embrace the universe that crushes us.
The sublime is the aesthetic experience of this dual condition: it makes us feel our smallness and, in the same movement, the greatness of what, within us, surpasses this smallness.
It is like a sensitive revelation of the paradoxical dignity of man.
The experience of the sublime also holds value in a world that tends to forget it.
For we are increasingly living in a humanized, controlled environment, tailored to our measure, from which the disproportionate, the immense, that which surpasses us, tends to disappear.
Our cities, our screens, our confined existences shield us from encountering what exceeds the human.
Yet this encounter has value: it displaces us, reminds us of our smallness, tears us away from the disproportion of our own importance.
The sublime is a lesson in humility, but a humility that does not belittle; on the contrary, it elevates us by placing us in the presence of what surpasses us.

A civilization that has lost all experience of the sublime, all contact with what exceeds it, would be a shriveled civilization, confined within its own measure, deprived of the elevation that the encounter with the immense provides.

Cultivating the experience of the sublime, arranging for encounters with what surpasses us — nature in its disproportion, the immensity of the sky, the power of the elements, but also the greatness of certain works, thoughts, and actions — is therefore essential to preserving a vital dimension of our humanity.
The sublime reminds us that we are not the measure of all things, that something surpasses us, and that in this very encounter, what we hold highest is revealed.

In a world that confines us to our own measure, that reduces everything to the human, the useful, the manageable, the experience of the sublime is like an open window onto the immense, a reminder of our intertwined smallness and greatness.
It may be one of the experiences that humanity needs most, and from which our time deprives us the most.

sentences: A civilization does not sustain itself; it only survives by transmitting what it holds most precious from one generation to the next — its knowledge, its values, its works, its ways of life.
Transmission is thus the vital act through which a civilization perpetuates itself, recreates itself in each generation, and escapes death.
However, this transmission, which was once almost naturally assured, has become difficult, uncertain, and threatened.
And this difficulty in transmitting is not a minor issue; it touches on the very survival of what we hold most precious, on the continuity of civilization itself.
What does it mean to transmit?
It is not just about communicating information or teaching techniques; it is about passing on a living heritage, a world of meaning, values, works, and ways of being from one generation to another.
Transmitting means giving to those who come after us what we have received from those who preceded us, placing them in a continuity, bequeathing them a world that they will make their own in turn.
It is an act of fidelity to the past and responsibility to the future, the link that connects generations in a continuous chain.
Without transmission, each generation would have to reinvent everything, start from scratch; it is through transmission that humanity accumulates, perpetuates itself, and does not keep starting over.
However, this transmission is currently made difficult by several factors.
The pace of change, first: in a world that is transforming so quickly, the legacy of past generations seems quickly outdated, surpassed, and worthless for a present that has broken away from it.
Why pass on what seems obsolete?

The rift between generations, next: the gap that separates them, the impression that young people live in a world so different that the experiences of the elders no longer concern them, makes transmission more challenging.

The devaluation of the past, finally: a culture focused on novelty, the present, and the future tends to despise heritage, to regard it as a burden rather than a treasure, and to value rupture over continuity.
This difficulty in transmitting has serious consequences that are poorly understood.

For what is not transmitted is lost; and a civilization that ceases to transmit itself would unravel, not through a sudden catastrophe, but through the silent erosion of what would no longer be bequeathed.

The accumulated knowledge, the works, the values, the ways of being that constitute a civilization survive only when transmitted; if we stop transmitting them, they fade away, not because they have been destroyed, but because they have not been passed on.
The breakdown of transmission is not just another educational issue; it poses a threat to the very continuity of civilization, an oblivion that erases what centuries have accumulated.
What is needed for transmission to be possible?

First, those who transmit must have something to pass on that they consider valuable, and they must want to transmit it; a generation that despises its own heritage, that sees nothing in it worth bequeathing, would transmit nothing.
Next, those who receive must be willing to accept, not rejecting by principle the heritage of past generations, and they must recognize that they have something to receive.

Finally, there must be places, institutions, and relationships where transmission can take place: schools, families, teachers, all those places where heritage is passed from one generation to another.
Transmission relies on a chain of goodwill, fidelity, and recognition, without which it breaks.
Caring for transmission is therefore one of the most essential and most neglected responsibilities of our time.

For we have inherited a world that we did not create, built and passed down by generations before us; and we have the responsibility to transmit it in turn, not to break the chain, not to squander a heritage that we only hold temporarily.
Transmitting what we hold most precious — knowledge, works, values, memory — ensures the survival of civilization, connecting it to its past and future, refusing to let it unravel into oblivion.

In a world that values rupture and despises heritage, rehabilitating transmission, taking care of it, wanting it, is perhaps one of the most urgent tasks for those who care about not losing civilization.
For a civilization does not only die from its catastrophes; it also dies, more silently, from ceasing to transmit itself.

sentences: Since the dawn of humanity, people have sought to conquer death, to achieve a form of immortality.

This quest has taken a thousand forms: belief in an afterlife, the pursuit of enduring glory, the desire to leave a lasting legacy, the passing on to descendants, and today, dreams of a science that would abolish death.
This stubbornness to want to conquer death, across ages and cultures, reveals something profound about our condition and about who we are.
What does this quest for immortality teach us about ourselves?
It first reveals the depth of our refusal of death, our desire to live, our revolt against finitude.
Humans are the only beings who know they will die, and this knowledge generates a refusal, a revolt, a quest to escape what burdens us.
This quest for immortality is the expression of our deepest desire: not to die, not to cease to be, to escape annihilation.
It testifies to humanity's attachment to life, its refusal of finitude, its revolt against the mortal condition.
In seeking immortality, humans express what is most fundamental to them: the desire to be, against the threat of non-being.
It also reveals the need for meaning, for permanence, for what lasts beyond the ephemeral.
For man is not content to exist in the moment; he aspires to what endures, to what escapes the flow of time, to a permanence that gives meaning to the ephemeral.
The quest for immortality is also a quest for meaning, for permanence, for what withstands the passage of time that takes everything away.

In the face of universal flight, of the impermanence of all things, man seeks what lasts, what endures, what escapes annihilation; and this quest expresses his need for meaning, his refusal of the insignificance of what passes without leaving a trace.
But this quest may also reveal an illusion, or at least an ambivalence.
For we have seen that immortality, if it were to be realized, could abolish what gives life its value — the finitude that makes time precious, the decisive choices, the intensity of what passes.
The quest for immortality, while it expresses a deep desire, could aim at something that, if realized, would disappoint, by taking away from life what makes it precious.
There is an ambivalence in this quest: we desire immortality, and yet immortality might not be the good we believe it to be, it could abolish the very meaning we seek.
Perhaps what we are really seeking is not to never die, but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it.
For there are forms of immortality that are not the abolition of death, but the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

Leaving behind a work, a mark, an influence that survives; contributing to something larger and more enduring than oneself; being part of a continuity that exceeds our individual existence: these are forms of transcending death that do not abolish it, but give our mortal life a significance that surpasses its duration.

This kind of immortality — not biological, but through meaning, work, mark, contribution — may be what we are truly seeking, one that answers our need for meaning and permanence without abolishing what gives value to finite life.
Not to never die, but for our passage to have a meaning that transcends it.
Thus, the quest for immortality, if understood correctly, may not aim so much at the abolition of death as at the transcendence of its finitude through meaning.

What we are really seeking may not be to never die — which would abolish the value of life — but to give our mortal life a meaning that transcends it, a significance that exceeds our duration, a mark that survives.
This kind of immortality is within our reach, not through science or a miracle, but through the way we live, through what we leave behind, through the meaning we give to our passage.
We will not conquer death; but we can make our mortal life have a meaning that transcends it, a value that survives, a mark that remains.

And perhaps this is the only immortality accessible to us, and the only one worth having: not the impossible and perhaps undesirable abolition of death, but the meaning we imbue our finite life with — this way of living that ensures that an existence, though mortal, will not have passed in vain.

sentences: Every year, I promise myself not to go to the sales.
And every year, I end up going anyway.
This year, the sales started on a Wednesday.
I arrived in town as soon as the stores opened.
There were already a lot of people.
People were crowding in front of the windows, looking for the best deals.
In the first store, I found a coat at half price.
I hadn't planned on it, but I bought it.
In the second store, I saw a perfect pair of shoes.
Another unplanned purchase!
After three hours, I had spent much more than I had planned.
When I got home, I looked at all my purchases.
I was happy, but a little guilty.
My husband looked at the bags and smiled.
"Sales again..." he said, without surprise.
Next year, I promise myself again: I won't go to the sales.
But I already know that I won't manage to do it.

sentences: This summer, we decided to take our dog, Rex, on vacation with us for the first time.
Before, we always left him at my parents' house during our trips.
But this year, we wanted to try something different.
The car ride lasted six hours.
Rex had never taken such a long trip.
He slept for half the journey, and he looked out the window the rest of the time, looking very interested.
Once we arrived, we found a rental that accepted dogs, near the sea.
On the first day, Rex discovered the beach.
He was running in all directions, completely excited.
He hesitated for a long time before entering the water.
Then, little by little, he approached the waves.
Finally, he loved swimming even more than we had imagined.
Every morning during the holidays, Rex waited for us at the door, ready to go back to the beach.
Back home, we decided that it would never be a vacation without him again.

sentences: Last month, I took an overnight train to visit my family, over a thousand kilometers from my home.
Usually, I take the plane, but this time, I wanted to try something different.
I had reserved a sleeper in a compartment for four people.
When I got on the train, two other passengers were already settled: a student and a businesswoman.
The fourth passenger, an elderly man, arrived just before departure, a bit out of breath.
At first, no one was really talking.
Everyone was looking at their phone or reading a book.
Around eleven o'clock, the elderly man offered to share the cookies he had brought.
The conversation started naturally.
He told us that he made this same trip every year, for thirty years, to visit his son.
We talked for almost two hours, before everyone fell asleep in their sleeper.
The train ran all night, with a soft, regular sound, almost soothing.
The next morning, I arrived rested, with the strange feeling of having experienced a little moment suspended in time.
I will probably make this train journey again, even though it's longer than flying.

alignments.french: pour rendre visite à son fils

sentences: Ten years ago, I placed my very first order online.

Many people around me said it wasn't safe.

I finally confirmed my order, hoping I hadn't made a mistake.
In the following days, I checked the package almost every day, curious and a little worried.
Four days later, the delivery person rang my doorbell with my package.
I opened the parcel with almost childlike excitement.
The book was exactly the one I had ordered.
Since that day, I shop online regularly, without any more fear.

sentences: Why does a song heard just once, twenty years ago, remain etched in our memory?
The neuroscientists studying this phenomenon have found interesting explanations.
Music activates several areas of the brain at the same time: those that manage emotions, memory, and even movement.
This multiple activation would explain why a song linked to a significant moment in our lives becomes almost impossible to forget.
The brain associates the melody with the emotion experienced at that specific moment.
This explains, for example, why a song heard during a first love, a funeral, or an important trip often remains forever linked to that event.
An even more astonishing phenomenon concerns people with severe memory disorders, such as certain forms of dementia.
Many of them, unable to recognize their own relatives, still remember the lyrics of songs learned in their youth.
This suggests that musical memory is somehow more deeply rooted than other types of memories, perhaps because it engages so many parts of the brain simultaneously.

Some teachers are already using this mechanism in the classroom: associating complex information with a simple melody surprisingly facilitates memorization, even for students who otherwise struggle to retain the same lesson presented in a purely verbal form.
These studies today open up interesting avenues, particularly for using music in the treatment of certain memory-related diseases.

sentences: Six months ago, I deactivated all my social media accounts for an entire month.
The idea came to me after a particularly exhausting week, when I felt like I was spending more time looking at my phone than actually living my own life.
The first week without these apps was more difficult than I expected.
I felt an almost physical absence, a desire to check a notification that no longer existed.
Then, gradually, something changed.
Without the endless scrolling of posts, I rediscovered time I didn't even know I had: to read, to cook longer, to call friends on the phone instead of just liking their photos.
By the third week, I noticed that I was sleeping better, probably because I wasn't looking at my phone right before closing my eyes.
When I reactivated my accounts at the end of the month, I was surprised to see how little I had actually missed, in reality, months of news and various posts.
Two friends, worried about not hearing from me, called me directly during this break, a mode of communication we had almost abandoned.
These conversations, longer and deeper than our usual online exchanges, reminded me of a form of friendship that social media had, without me really realizing it, quietly replaced.
I haven't deleted my accounts permanently.
But I now regularly give myself breaks, remembering what that month had given me.

sentences: Few experiences are as revealing of cultural differences as attending a comedy show in a foreign country, where you understand every word spoken, yet still don't always grasp the humor.
This phenomenon can be explained by the deeply contextual nature of humor, which rarely relies on the simple literal meaning of words.
A good portion of successful jokes rely on specific cultural references, shared social habits, or implications that require an implicit understanding of the context to be perceived as funny.
Certain forms of humor, such as irony or self-deprecation, also vary significantly from one culture to another in their social acceptability.
What constitutes a charming mark of humility in one culture may be perceived in another as a concerning sign of a lack of self-confidence, which radically changes the reception of the joke itself.

The narrative structure of humor also differs according to cultural traditions: some cultures favor a quick and explicit punchline, while others appreciate a more subtle humor based on the implicit and the unspoken, which can be difficult for someone used to a more direct style to perceive.

This difficulty in culturally translating humor explains why so many comedies, despite being very popular in their country of origin, often fail to achieve the same success once exported, even with a technically faithful translation of the dialogues.
Ultimately, humor is never really translated word for word; it requires a true cultural transposition, much more demanding than a simple linguistic translation.

sentences: Fashion occupies a strange position in our culture: celebrated in museums as a form of artistic expression in its own right, but also criticized, at the same time, as a purely commercial industry, focused on profit rather than true creation.
This ambiguity is not new.

Since the beginnings of haute couture, some designers have always claimed an artist's status, while other players in the industry fully embraced their commercial logic, without any particular artistic pretension.

The argument in favor of fashion's artistic status is based on solid elements: a haute couture collection often requires hundreds of hours of manual labor, undeniable formal creativity, and the ability to translate abstract ideas into concrete forms.
In this regard, it does not seem fundamentally different from other forms of art recognized as such.

The opposing argument rightly emphasizes the eminently commercial dimension of the industry: unlike a traditional work of art, a fashion garment is designed, from the outset, to be sold in quantity, produced according to industrial logic, often in manufacturing conditions far removed from any artistic ideal.
Perhaps the most honest answer is to reject this overly binary opposition.
Contemporary fashion inextricably mixes an authentic creative dimension with an acknowledged commercial logic, without one necessarily negating the other.
Some garments clearly fall into one or the other category; most, in reality, are situated somewhere in between, bearing both the mark of an aesthetic vision and the constraints of a global market.

sentences: From then on, she drank vinegar to lose weight, developed a slight dry cough, and completely lost her appetite.
It was hard for Charles to leave Tostes after four years of living there and just when he was starting to settle in.
If it was necessary, however!
He took her to Rouen to see her former teacher.
It was a nervous illness: she needed a change of scenery.
After turning this way and that, Charles learned that there was a large town named Yonville-l’Abbaye in the Neufchâtel district, whose doctor, a Polish refugee, had just fled the previous week.

Then he wrote to the local pharmacist to find out the population number, the distance to the nearest colleague, how much his predecessor earned per year, etc.; and, as the answers were satisfactory, he decided to move in the spring if Emma's health did not improve.
One day, as she was tidying up a drawer in preparation for her departure, she pricked her fingers on something.
It was a piece of wire from her wedding bouquet.
The orange blossoms were yellow with dust, and the satin ribbons, edged with silver, were fraying at the edges.
She threw it into the fire.
It ignited faster than dry straw.
Then it was like a red bush on the ashes, slowly eating away.
She watched it burn.
The small cardboard berries burst, the wires twisted, the trim melted; and the paper corollas, shriveled, swayed along the plate like black butterflies, before finally flying up the chimney.

sentences: These thoughts came back to me as I considered the coal riches accumulated in this part of the earth's massif.
They will undoubtedly never be uncovered.
Exploiting these remote mines would require too great sacrifices.

However, we were walking, and I alone among my companions forgot the length of the road as I became lost in geological considerations.
The temperature remained roughly what it was during our passage through the lavas and schists.
Only, my sense of smell was affected by a very strong odor of hydrogen proto-carbide.
I immediately recognized, in this gallery, the presence of a significant amount of this dangerous fluid that miners call firedamp, which has often caused terrible disasters due to its explosions.

sentences: However, I was returning from a difficult journey, tired and eager for rest.
I longed only to see my country, my friends, my little home in the Jardin des Plantes, my dear and precious collections!
But nothing could hold me back.
I forgot everything: fatigue, friends, collections, and I accepted the offer from the American government without further thought.
Besides, I thought, every road leads back to Europe, and the Unicorn will be kind enough to carry me towards the shores of France!

This worthy creature will allow itself to be captured in the seas of Europe -- for my personal enjoyment -- and I don't want to bring back less than half a meter of its ivory halberd to the Natural History Museum.
But in the meantime, I had to search for this narwhal in the northern Pacific Ocean; which, in order to return to France, meant taking the path of the antipodes.
"Counsel!" I shouted in an impatient voice.
Counsel was my servant.

A devoted boy who accompanied me on all my journeys; a good Flemish man whom I loved and who returned my affection, a phlegmatic being by nature, regular by principle, eager by habit, rarely surprised by life's surprises, very skilled with his hands, fit for any service, and, despite his name, never giving advice -- even when it wasn't asked for.
By interacting with the scholars of our little world at the Jardin des Plantes, Conseil had come to know something.

I had in him a specialist, very knowledgeable about classification in natural history, navigating the entire hierarchy of groups, classes, subclasses, orders, families, genera, subgenera, species, and varieties with the agility of an acrobat.
But his knowledge stopped there.
Classifying was his life, and he didn't know any more than that.
Very well-versed in the theory of classification, but lacking in practice, he wouldn't have been able to distinguish, I believe, a sperm whale from a whale!
And yet, what a brave and worthy young man!

It seems to me that the first concern of Bonapartist justice should have been to release those who were imprisoned by royalist justice.
--Don't accuse recklessly, my dear Mr. Morrel, Villefort replied; we must proceed legally in all matters.
The order of incarceration came from above, so the order of release must also come from above.
Now, Napoleon has only just returned for barely fifteen days; the letters of abolition must also just be sent out.
--But, Morrel asked, is there no way to expedite the formalities now that we are triumphant?
I have some friends, some influence; I can obtain the lifting of the order.
--There has been no order.
--Then the detention order.
--In political matters, there is no detention register; sometimes governments have an interest in making a person disappear without leaving a trace: detention notes would guide searches.
--It may have been like that under the Bourbons, but now....

It's always been like this throughout history, my dear Mr. Morrel; governments come and go, and they are all alike; the prison system established under Louis XIV is still in operation today, near the Bastille.
The Emperor has always been stricter about the management of his prisons than the Great King himself; and the number of inmates whose records leave no trace is incalculable.
Such kindness would have diverted from certainties, and Morrel had no suspicions at all.

sentences: A neighborhood visit.
On December 2, the intensity of the cold had decreased.
These parhelion phenomena were a symptom that a meteorologist could not have mistaken.
They noted the presence of a certain amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, and indeed, the barometer dropped slightly, while the thermometer rose to fifteen degrees above zero (-90 centigrade).
Although this cold still seemed harsh in any region of the temperate zone, professional winterers endured it easily.
Moreover, the atmosphere was calm.
Lieutenant Hobson, having observed that the upper layers of frozen snow had softened, ordered the clearing of the outer areas of the enclosure.
Mac Nap and his men undertook this task with courage, and in a few days it was successfully completed.
At the same time, the buried traps were uncovered, and they were set again.
Numerous tracks proved that fur-bearing game was gathering around the cape, and, with the ground offering it no food, it would easily be lured into the traps.
Following the advice of the hunter Marbre, a reindeer trap was also built, using the method of the Eskimos.
It was a pit about ten feet wide in all directions and about twelve feet deep.
A board acting as a seesaw, which could lift itself by its own weight, covered it in such a way as to completely conceal it.
The animal, attracted by the herbs and branches placed at the end of the board, was inevitably plunged into the pit, from which it could no longer escape.
It is understood that, with this seesaw system, the trap would automatically reset, and that once a reindeer was caught, others could fall into it as well.

Marbre encountered no other difficulty in setting up his trap than breaking through very hard ground; however, he was quite surprised — and Jasper Hobson was no less so — when the pickaxe, after passing through four to five feet of earth and sand, hit a layer of snow below, as hard as rock, which seemed to be very thick.

"It must be, said Lieutenant Hobson, after observing this geological arrangement, that this part of the coastline was subjected, many years ago, to extreme cold for a very long period of time; then, the sands and earth must have gradually covered the ice mass, presumably resting on a granite bed.

sentences: Protésilas listened to all these praises with a dry, distracted, and disdainful air, like a man who knows he deserves even greater ones, and who is too gracious to allow himself to be praised.
There was a flatterer who took the liberty of speaking to him in his ear, to say something amusing against the authority that Mentor was trying to establish.
Protésilas smiled; the whole assembly immediately began to laugh, although most could not yet know what had been said.
But Protésilas soon resumed his severe and haughty demeanor, and everyone fell back into fear and silence.

Several nobles were looking for the moment when Protésilas might turn towards them and listen to them: they appeared moved and embarrassed; it was because they had requests to make of him; their pleading posture spoke for them; they looked as submissive as a mother at the feet of the altars when she asks the gods for the healing of her only son.
Everyone seemed pleased, touched, filled with admiration for Protésilas, although they all harbored an unrelenting rage against him in their hearts.
At that moment, Hégésippe entered, seized Protésilas's sword, and declared to him, on behalf of the king, that he was going to take him to the island of Samos.
At these words, all the arrogance of this favorite fell away, like a rock that detaches from the top of a steep mountain.

There he was, trembling and disturbed, throwing himself at Hégésippe's feet; he cried, hesitated, stammered, trembled; he embraced the knees of this man whom he had not deemed worthy of even a glance an hour earlier.
All those who had been flattering him, seeing him lost and without resources, turned their flattery into merciless insults.
Hégésippe did not want to give him time either to say his final goodbyes to his family or to take some secret writings.
Everything was seized and taken to the king.
Timocrate was arrested at the same time: and his surprise was extreme; for he believed that being at odds with Protésilas, he could not be caught up in his downfall.
They set off in a ship that had been prepared.
They arrived at Samos.
Hégésippe left these two unfortunate men there; and, to add to their misfortune, he left them together.

There, they furiously reproached each other for the crimes they had committed, which were the cause of their downfall: they found themselves without hope of seeing Salente again, condemned to live far from their wives and children; I won't even mention their friends, as they had none.
They were being taken to an unknown land, where they would have no other means of living but their labor, they who had spent so many years in luxury and extravagance.
Like two wild beasts, they were always ready to tear each other apart.

sentences: In France, about one in three households consists of a single person.
This proportion has doubled in fifty years, and it continues to rise.
This figure is often commented on in a worried tone.
It would be better to look at it more calmly, as it mixes two different realities.
Living alone is a housing situation.
It is sometimes chosen and appreciated: freedom, calm, absence of daily compromises.
Many people living alone have a rich social life.
Isolation is something else.
It is the absence of regular relationships and support, and it can perfectly exist within a couple or a family.
This distinction is important because the documented effects on health concern isolation, not the fact of living alone.
Research is quite convergent: prolonged isolation increases cardiovascular risks, promotes depression, and is comparable, in some studies, to well-known risk factors like smoking.
The most affected populations are not always the ones we imagine.
Yes, elderly widows.
But also young adults who have just arrived in a city, and caregivers who look after a sick relative and no longer have time for themselves.
Effective responses do not consist of telling people to 'go out more'.
They create opportunities: associations, neighborhood activities, shared gardens, third places, organized visits.
What makes these initiatives effective is their regularity.
A one-time event is not enough.
Living alone is therefore neither good nor bad in itself.
What matters is the number of people who would notice your absence.

sentences: Light pollution is a relatively recent issue that has long been considered secondary.
Research conducted over the past twenty years has changed this perspective.
Artificial night lighting has significantly increased worldwide, and nearly the entire European population now lives under a sky where the Milky Way is invisible.
The documented effects concern a large part of living beings.
For insects, light acts like a trap.
They circle around light sources until exhaustion, do not reproduce, and become easy prey.
It is estimated that night lighting is among the causes of the decline of insects.
For migratory birds, which navigate partly by the stars, illuminated cities are disorienting.
Collisions with illuminated buildings are regularly observed.
Bats, which hunt at night, avoid lit areas and thus lose hunting territories.
Plants themselves are affected: trees located under streetlights keep their leaves longer in autumn.
In humans, night light disrupts melatonin production and sleep quality.
What makes this topic special is that it is easy to fix — much more so than most environmental issues.
Turning off a light requires neither technology nor heavy investment.
It even reduces the bill.
Many French municipalities have already implemented a nighttime light-out policy, with no increase in crime observed, contrary to the expressed fears.
Few ecological measures are cheaper and act as quickly.
It literally just takes pressing a switch.

sentences: Our time has made utility a sovereign value.
An activity, a study, an expense, even a life, is justified by what it serves; what serves no purpose is suspect, called to account, and threatened with disappearance due to lack of profitability.

This demand for utility, which seems like simple common sense, actually exercises a discreet tyranny, as it ends up measuring everything by the service it provides, and devaluing everything that would be valuable in itself.
However, a civilization that would no longer recognize anything but the useful would lose what precisely gives value to existence.
First, it must be understood that utility is, by nature, a relative criterion: one thing is useful to another, with a view to an end that transcends it.
The hammer is useful to the nail, the nail to the board, the board to the house.
But this chain of means must stop somewhere, at something that is not useful to something else, but that is valuable in itself, and for which everything else is useful.
If everything were only useful, the chain would be endless and aimless; utility itself would have no meaning, lacking an end that is not, in turn, a mere means.
Therefore, the useful presupposes, to have meaning, something that escapes utility.
This something refers to those experiences and goods that are valuable in themselves: friendship, beauty, knowledge sought for its own sake, contemplation, play, joy.
None of them 'serves' any purpose in the strict sense; we do not cultivate a friendship for what it brings, nor do we contemplate a landscape for its yield.
These things are ends, not means, and it is for them, ultimately, that everything else is organized.
To consider them useless because they serve no other purpose is to reverse the hierarchy: it is to take means for ends, and to sacrifice what is valuable for what is valuable only for something else.
Yet it is this reversal that the tyranny of the useful enacts.
It demands that beauty justify itself by its economic utility, knowledge by its applications, and leisure by its function of recuperation in service of work.
Everything must serve, and what does not serve must prove that it serves nonetheless, or it risks being abolished.
Thus, a society entirely devoted to the useful eventually loses sight of what all this serves, having forgotten the non-useful ends for which utility had meaning.
It produces and busies itself without knowing why, with activity having become its own justification.
This drift even affects our understanding of human life.
To require every existence to justify itself by its utility is to deny that a life can have worth in itself, independent of what it produces or brings in.
It is the slope that leads to measuring beings by their output, to considering those who no longer produce as a burden, and to recognizing dignity only in useful life.
However, a life is not a means; it is, if there is something that has worth in itself, that very something.
Reducing existence to its utility is to miss what, in it, transcends all utility.
Defending the gratuitous against the tyranny of the useful is therefore not advocating for idleness or waste.

It is to remind us that utility is not the supreme value, but a subordinate order, which only makes sense in service of ends that, in themselves, serve no purpose because they are what everything serves.

A civilization may be judged less by what it produces than by what it knows how to preserve as gratuitous: the space it allows for beauty, for disinterested thought, for connections that yield nothing, for everything that, while serving no purpose, makes life worth living.
For what has no price, in the sense that it cannot be exchanged for money, is also what has no price in the sense that nothing is worth it.

sentences: After years of traditional travel, I decided last year to completely change the way I travel.

Previously, my vacations always followed the same pattern: visiting as many monuments as possible in the shortest amount of time, checking off a list of must-see places, and then returning exhausted, with the paradoxical feeling of needing a vacation after my vacation.
Last year, I chose a different approach: to stay an entire month in a single village, without a specific itinerary, without a list of things to see absolutely.
This change initially unsettled me a bit.
In the first few days, I felt a sort of guilt about 'doing nothing,' being used to filling each day with visits.
Then, gradually, I discovered another way to travel.
I got to know the local merchants, understood the local habits, and slowed down enough to really observe what was around me rather than just passing through it.
This slower mode of travel also corresponds to what is now called sustainable tourism, which limits frequent travel and favors a reduced impact on the places visited.
Strangely, I remember this month spent in the village much better than many shorter and busier trips taken in previous years.
Slowness, contrary to what I feared, produced richer and more precise memories than the rapid accumulation of visits I practiced before.
I don't completely deny my previous travels, which introduced me to many beautiful places.
But this new approach, slower and deeper, offered me something that my previous trips had never managed to give me: a true feeling of having lived somewhere, even if just for a month.

sentences: Forgiveness is regarded as a great virtue, a transcendence of vengeance, a liberation for both the one who grants it and the one who receives it.
But as soon as we reflect on it, forgiveness reveals itself to be riddled with formidable paradoxes.
Are there unforgivable offenses, or can everything be forgiven?
Does forgiveness have meaning if it is always owed, or does it precisely imply that it could be refused?
Must the guilty party repent in order to be forgiven, or can forgiveness be unconditional?
These questions, far from being trivial, touch on what is most profound and most difficult about forgiveness.
Let's first consider the question of unforgivable offenses.
One viewpoint holds that everything can be forgiven, that there is no offense that forgiveness cannot reach, and that refusing to forgive would be a failure of virtue.
This position has its merits: it affirms the unlimited power of forgiveness, its ability to overcome the worst.
But it faces a formidable objection: some offenses seem so egregious that forgiving them would amount to trivializing them, betraying the victims, and erasing the horror.
Can we, should we forgive extreme crimes, those that go beyond all measure?
And who could do it?
Certainly not third parties, who have not suffered the offense; and the victims themselves, when they are no longer there to forgive, leave the offense in a kind of irredeemable state.
It seems that there are offenses that exceed forgiveness, not because forgiveness is limited, but because forgiving them would be an injustice to what they have destroyed.
Here we encounter a first paradox: forgiveness may only make sense in the face of what seems unforgivable.
For forgiving what is easily excusable, a minor fault, a slight offense, is not really forgiveness; it is excusing, forgetting, letting it go.
True forgiveness only begins where excuse is no longer sufficient, in the face of a real, serious fault that could legitimately provoke resentment.
Forgiveness presupposes the fault, a fault that cannot be excused, and it precisely consists of not demanding the punishment that this fault would deserve, renouncing legitimate resentment.
Thus, true forgiveness is only exercised in the face of what, in a sense, does not deserve it; it is gratuitous, it exceeds what is owed.
If it were always owed, it would no longer be forgiveness, but justice; it is because it could be refused that it has the value of a gift.
A second paradox concerns the condition of forgiveness.
Must the offender repent, acknowledge their wrongdoing, and ask for forgiveness in order to be forgiven?
This condition seems reasonable: how can one forgive someone who feels no regret, persists in their wrongdoing, and does not ask for forgiveness?
Forgiveness granted to someone who does not repent seems futile, even complicit.
And yet, subordinating forgiveness to repentance may distort it: for then forgiveness becomes conditional, deserved, almost owed to the one who repents, and it loses its gratuitousness.
The highest, most difficult form of forgiveness might be that which is granted unconditionally, without waiting for repentance, as a pure grace.
But does such unconditional forgiveness not risk trivializing wrongdoing, freeing the offender from any self-reflection?
The paradox is here: conditional forgiveness may not be true forgiveness, but unconditional forgiveness risks injustice.
These paradoxes do not have simple solutions, and it would be presumptuous to claim to resolve them.

But they reveal the profound nature of forgiveness: that it is neither a right nor an oblivion, neither justice nor complacency, but something excessive, gratuitous, almost impossible, which only makes sense in the face of what seems to reject it.
True forgiveness is difficult precisely because it is not owed, because it is exercised in the face of what could legitimately call for resentment, because it exceeds justice without abolishing it.

It consists neither in excusing wrongdoing, nor in forgetting it, nor in renouncing justice, but in overcoming personal resentment, in not allowing the wrongdoing to poison indefinitely the one who has suffered it.
What remains, after all these paradoxes, is that forgiveness, if it is possible, is a liberation, but a liberation primarily for the one who forgives.
For resentment, hatred, and the desire for revenge first poison the one who harbors them; forgiveness, by renouncing them, frees the one who grants it from the poison of their own bitterness.

Forgiveness does not erase the wrongdoing, does not bring justice, does not resurrect what has been destroyed; but it frees the one who forgives from the grip of the suffered wrongdoing, refusing to let the received harm continue to dominate them through resentment.
In this sense, even in the face of what seems unforgivable, a form of forgiveness can be a victory: not over the wrongdoing, which remains, but over its power to trap us in hatred.

To forgive may not be to absolve the guilty, but to free oneself — and perhaps it is in this liberation that the deepest and most accessible meaning of forgiveness lies, one that can never be an acquittal regarding certain wrongs.

sentences: I regret not having anything better to offer you," said Mr. Fogg to Fix, who bowed without replying.
The police inspector felt a sort of humiliation in taking advantage of Mr. Fogg's kindness.
"Surely, he thought, he's a very polite rogue, but he's still a rogue!"
At three ten, the sails were raised.
The English flag was flying at the bow of the schooner.
The passengers were sitting on the deck.
Mr. Fogg and Mrs. Aouda took a last look at the quay to see if Passepartout would appear.

Fix was not without apprehension, as chance could have led the unfortunate boy he had treated so indignantly right to this spot, and then an explanation would have erupted, from which the detective would not have come out in his favor.
But the Frenchman did not show up, and undoubtedly, the numbing narcotic still had him under its influence.

sentences: The baroness stood up quickly.
She was about to go to the study to inform her daughter when Danglars stopped her by the arm.
"Let go," he said.
She looked at him in surprise.
Monte-Cristo pretended not to have seen this little scene.
Albert entered; he was very handsome and very cheerful.
He greeted the baroness with ease, Danglars with familiarity, and Monte-Cristo with affection; then turning to the baroness,
"Would you allow me, madam," he said to her, "to ask how Mlle Danglars is doing?"
"Very well, sir," Danglars replied quickly, "she is currently playing music in her small parlor with Mr. Cavalcanti."
Albert maintained his calm and indifferent demeanor; perhaps he felt some inner annoyance, but he sensed Monte-Cristo's gaze fixed on him.
"Mr. Cavalcanti has a very beautiful tenor voice," he said, "and Mlle Eugénie has a magnificent soprano, not to mention that she plays the piano like Thalberg.
It must be a lovely concert.

sentences: On the morning of April 16, the sleds hitched in front of the gate were just waiting for the travelers.
Captain Craventy, having gathered the men who made up the detachment, addressed them with a few friendly words.
Above all, he urged them to maintain constant unity in the face of the dangers they were about to face.
Obedience to their leaders was an essential condition for the success of this mission, a work of selflessness and dedication.
Cheers greeted the captain's speech.
Then the goodbyes were quickly said, and everyone took their place in the sled that had been assigned to them in advance.
Jasper Hobson and Sergeant Long were at the front.
Mrs. Paulina Barnett and Madge followed them, with Madge skillfully handling the long Eskimo whip finished with a strap of hardened nerve.
Thomas Black and one of the soldiers, the Canadian Petersen, formed the third rank of the caravan.
The other sleds then passed by, occupied by the soldiers and the women.
Corporal Joliffe and Mrs. Joliffe were at the rear.
Following Jasper Hobson's orders, each driver was to maintain their designated position and keep their distance as much as possible to avoid any confusion.
And indeed, the collision of these sleds, launched at full speed, could have led to some unfortunate accident.

sentences: At the Barrière du Trône, they encountered Bertuccio: he was waiting there, motionless like a sentinel at his post.
Monte-Cristo leaned his head out of the carriage window, exchanged a few words with him in a low voice, and the steward disappeared.
"Count, said Emmanuel as he reached the Place Royale, please have me dropped off at my door, so that my wife won't have a moment's worry about either you or me.
--If it weren't ridiculous to show off one's triumph, said Morrel, I would invite the Count to come into our home, but the Count surely has trembling hearts to reassure as well.
Here we are, Emmanuel, let's greet our friend and let him continue on his way.

--One moment, said Monte-Cristo, don't deprive me of my two companions all at once; go back to your lovely wife, to whom I charge you to send my best regards, and accompany me to the Champs-Élysées, Morrel.
--Perfect, said Maximilien, especially since I have business in your area, Count.
--Will they wait for you for lunch? asked Emmanuel.
--No, said the young man.
The carriage door closed, and the vehicle continued on its way.
"See how I have brought you good luck, said Morrel when he was alone with the Count.
Did you not think of that?

A rush of joyful blood quickly rose to the cheeks of the sick woman; for the name just spoken by the count took away the last bit of distrust that he had inspired in her.
Maximilien!... repeated Valentine, so sweet did this name seem to her to pronounce; Maximilien! has he confessed everything to you?

sentences: But what is Mr. de Villefort telling me? asked Monte-Cristo; and what an incomprehensible disgrace?...
"Incomprehensible, that's the word!" replied the public prosecutor, shrugging his shoulders, "a whim of an old man!"
"Is there no way to make him change this decision?"
"Indeed there is," said Mme de Villefort; "and it even depends on my husband that this will, instead of being made to the detriment of Valentine, is made in her favor instead."

The count, seeing that the two spouses were starting to speak in riddles, took on a distracted air and looked with the deepest attention and the most marked approval at Édouard, who was pouring ink into the birds' drinking fountain.

"My dear," said Villefort, responding to his wife, "you know that I don't like to position myself as a patriarch at home, and that I've never believed that the fate of the universe depended on a nod from me.
However, it is important that my decisions are respected in my family, and that the folly of an old man and the whim of a child do not overturn a plan that has been settled in my mind for many years.
The baron d'Épinay was my friend, you know, and an alliance with his son was very suitable.

sentences: And as he spoke these words in a muffled and almost choked voice, Mr. de Villefort staggered toward the door, which the usher opened for him with a mechanical motion.

The entire assembly remained silent and stunned by this revelation and confession, which brought such a terrible conclusion to the various events that had stirred the Parisian high society for the past fifteen days.
"Well," said Beauchamp, "let them now say that the drama is not in human nature!"
"Indeed," said Château-Renaud, "I would much rather end like Mr. de Morcerf: a gunshot seems gentle compared to such a catastrophe."
"And besides, it kills," said Beauchamp.
"And I who had briefly considered marrying his daughter," said Debray.
"Did she do well to die, my God, the poor child!"
"The session is adjourned, gentlemen," said the president, "and the case is postponed to the next session."
"The matter must be re-examined and entrusted to another magistrate."
As for Andrea, still as calm and much more interesting, he left the room escorted by the gendarmes, who inadvertently showed him respect.
"Well, what do you think of that, my good man?" asked Debray of the city sergeant, slipping a louis into his hand.

sentences: Well, this is what you call taking things in good spirit.
And everyone formed a circle around the fire again, while Diavolaccio moved away.
Carlini ate and drank as if nothing had happened.
The bandits looked at him in astonishment, not understanding this impassiveness, when they heard a heavy step behind them echoing on the ground.
They turned around and saw Diavolaccio holding the young girl in his arms.
Her head was thrown back, and her long hair hung down to the ground.
As they entered the circle of light cast by the fire, one could see the paleness of the young girl and the paleness of the bandit.
This appearance had something so strange and so solemn about it that everyone stood up, except for Carlini, who remained seated and continued to eat and drink as if nothing was happening around him.
Diavolaccio continued to advance in the deepest silence and laid Rita at the captain's feet.
Then everyone could recognize the cause of the young girl's paleness and the bandit's paleness: Rita had a knife buried to the hilt beneath her left breast.
All eyes turned to Carlini: the sheath was empty at his belt.
Ah! ah! said the chief, now I understand why Carlini stayed behind.
Every wild nature is capable of appreciating a strong action; although perhaps none of the bandits would have done what Carlini had just done, they all understood what he had done.
--Well, said Carlini, getting up and approaching the corpse, his hand on the grip of one of his pistols, is there anyone left who disputes this woman with me?

sentences: In an instant, Debray had dismounted and found himself at the door.
He offered his hand to the baroness, who made an imperceptible gesture as she descended, noticeable only to Monte-Cristo.

But the count missed nothing, and in that gesture, he saw a small white note glimmering, as imperceptible as the gesture itself, which passed, with an ease that indicated the habit of this maneuver, from Mme Danglars' hand to that of the minister's secretary.
Behind his wife, the banker descended, pale as if he had emerged from a tomb instead of from his carriage.

Mme Danglars cast a quick, investigative glance around her that only Monte-Cristo could understand, in which she took in the courtyard, the peristyle, and the façade of the house; then, suppressing a slight emotion that would surely have shown on her face if it had been permissible for her face to pale, she ascended the steps while saying to Morrel:
"Sir, if you were one of my friends, I would ask you if your horse is for sale."
Morrel gave a smile that closely resembled a grimace and turned to Monte-Cristo, as if to ask him to help him out of the embarrassment he was in.
The count understood him.
"Ah! madam," he replied, "why is this request not directed to me?
"With you, sir," said the baroness, "one has no right to desire anything, for one is too sure of getting it.
So it was to Mr. Morrel.
"Unfortunately," the count replied, "I am a witness that Mr. Morrel cannot part with his horse, as his honor is at stake in keeping it.

sentences: Oh! The trees were all cut down.
Come, and you'll see him at work.
After a quarter of an hour of walking, on the other side of the promontory that formed the small natural harbor, I saw Hans at work; just a few more steps, and I was close to him.

To my great surprise, a half-finished raft was lying on the sand; it was made of beams from a special wood, and a large number of planks, curves, and various pairs were literally strewn across the ground.
There was enough there to build an entire fleet.
My uncle, I exclaimed, what is this wood?
It's pine, fir, birch, all the species of northern conifers, mineralized under the action of seawater.
Is it possible?
This is what is called "surtarbrandur" or fossil wood.
But then, like lignites, it must have the hardness of stone, and it won't be able to float?
Sometimes that happens; there are some woods that have become true anthracites; but others, like these, have only undergone the beginning of fossil transformation.
Look instead, my uncle added, throwing one of these precious wrecks into the sea.
The piece of wood, after disappearing, resurfaced and swayed with the undulations of the waves.
"Are you convinced?" said my uncle.
"Convinced mainly that this is unbelievable!"

The next evening, thanks to the guide's skill, the raft was finished; it was ten feet long and five feet wide; the beams of surtarbrandur, connected by strong ropes, provided a solid surface, and once launched, this makeshift boat floated peacefully on the waters of the Lidenbrock Sea.

sentences: The old maid had died during the winter.
No one was concerned about this matter anymore; I alone kept thinking about it incessantly.
What had they done with this woman? Had she fled through the woods!
Had she been taken in somewhere and kept in a hospital without anyone being able to get any information from her?
Nothing eased my doubts; but gradually, time calmed the worry in my heart.
Now, in the following autumn, the woodcocks passed in droves; and since my gout was giving me a bit of a break, I dragged myself to the forest.
I had already killed four or five long-billed birds when I shot one that disappeared into a ditch full of branches.
I had to go down there to retrieve my bird.
I found it fallen next to a skull.
And suddenly, the memory of the madwoman hit me in the chest like a punch.
Many others had perished in these woods, perhaps in that sinister year; but I don't know why, I was sure, sure, I tell you, that I was encountering the skull of that miserable maniac.
And suddenly I understood, I guessed everything.

They had abandoned her on that mattress, in the cold and deserted forest; and, true to her fixed idea, she had let herself die under the thick and light duvet of the snow, without moving her arm or leg.
Then the wolves had devoured her.
And the birds had made their nest with the wool from her torn bed.
I kept this sad remains.
And I wish that our sons never see war again.

sentences: Thank you, sir, Monte-Cristo said with a smile; my steward has already been instructed to rent a box in each of them.
And is your steward also a Nubian, a mute? Debray asked.
No, sir, he is simply a compatriot of yours, if a Corsican can be considered a compatriot of anyone: but you know him, Monsieur de Morcerf.

Exactly, and you saw him at my place the day I had the honor of hosting you for lunch.
He is a very brave man, who has been a bit of a soldier, a bit of a smuggler, a bit of everything one can be, really.
I wouldn't even swear that he hasn't had some run-ins with the police over a trifle, something like a knife fight.
And you chose this honest citizen of the world as your steward, Monsieur the Count? Debray asked, how much does he steal from you each year?

Then, Château-Renaud said, you have a fully staffed house: you have a hotel on the Champs-Élysées, servants, a steward, all you need now is a mistress.

sentences: And the count, leaning his head out of the window, let out a small cry of excitement that gave wings to the horses; they were no longer running, they were flying.
The carriage rolled like thunder over the royal pavement, and everyone turned to see this blazing meteor pass by.

Ali, repeating this cry, smiled, showing his white teeth, gripping the foaming reins in his strong hands, urging the horses on, whose beautiful manes were scattered in the wind; Ali, the child of the desert, was in his element, and with his dark face, fiery eyes, and snow-white burnous, he seemed, amidst the dust he was raising, the genius of the simoon and the god of the hurricane.
"There, said Morcerf, is a pleasure I didn't know, it's the pleasure of speed."
And the last clouds on his brow dissipated, as if the air he was cutting through carried those clouds away with it.
"But where on earth do you find such horses? asked Albert.
Do you have them made on purpose?
"Exactly, said the count.
Six years ago, I found in Hungary a famous stallion renowned for its speed; I bought it for I don't remember how much: it was Bertuccio who paid.
In the same year, it had thirty-two offspring.

It's all this progeny from the same father that we are going to review; they are all alike, black, without a single spot, except for a star on the forehead, because for this privileged stallion, mares were chosen, just as favorites are chosen for pashas.
It's wonderful!...
But tell me, count, what are you doing with all these horses?
You see, I'm traveling with them.

sentences: From the lower part of my balloon, which is hermetically sealed, two tubes emerge separated by a small gap.
One originates in the middle of the upper layers of hydrogen gas, the other in the middle of the lower layers.
These two pipes are equipped at intervals with strong rubber joints, which allow them to adapt to the oscillations of the aerostat.
They both descend to the basket and disappear into a cylindrical iron box, which is called a heat box.
It is closed at both ends by two strong discs made of the same metal.

The pipe coming from the lower region of the balloon enters this cylindrical box through the bottom disc; it penetrates there and then takes the shape of a helical coil whose overlapping rings occupy almost the entire height of the box.
Before exiting, the coil goes into a small cone, whose concave base, shaped like a spherical cap, is directed downward.
It is through the top of this cone that the second pipe emerges, and it goes, as I told you, into the upper layers of the balloon.
The spherical cap of the small cone is made of platinum, in order not to melt under the action of the blowtorch.
For the blowtorch is placed at the bottom of the iron box, in the middle of the helical coil, and the tip of its flame will slightly lick this cap.
You know, gentlemen, what a radiator designed to heat apartments is.
You know how it works.
The air in the apartment is forced to pass through the pipes, and it is returned at a higher temperature.
Now, what I just described to you is, in fact, just a radiator.
Indeed, what will happen?
Once the burner is lit, the hydrogen in the coil and the concave cone heats up and quickly rises through the pipe that leads it to the upper regions of the balloon.

A vacuum forms below, attracting the gas from the lower regions, which in turn heats up and is continuously replaced; thus, an extremely rapid current of gas is established in the pipes and the coil, exiting the balloon, returning to it, and constantly overheating.

sentences: He didn't need to call out to them, as all the mouths in the crowd were open, as if to drink in his words.

Tuvache, next to him, listened with wide eyes; Mr. Derozerais, from time to time, gently closed his eyelids; and further away, the pharmacist, with his son Napoléon between his legs, cupped his hand to his ear to catch every single syllable.
The other jury members slowly nodded their chins in their vests, in a sign of approval.
The firefighters at the foot of the platform rested on their bayonets, and Binet, motionless, kept his elbow out, with the tip of his sword raised in the air.
He might have been hearing, but he must not have seen anything, due to the visor of his helmet that was hanging down over his nose.
Nevertheless, his lieutenant, the younger son of Mr. Tuvache, had exaggerated his even more, as he wore an enormous one that wobbled on his head, with a piece of his Indian scarf sticking out.
He smiled beneath it with a childlike sweetness, and his small pale face, where drops were streaming down, had an expression of pleasure, exhaustion, and sleep.
The square up to the houses was packed with people.
You could see people leaning out of every window, others standing in every doorway, and Justin, in front of the pharmacy's display, seemed completely absorbed in what he was watching.
Despite the silence, Mr. Lieuvain's voice was lost in the air.

It reached you in fragments of phrases, interrupted here and there by the noise of chairs in the crowd; then suddenly, behind you, a long lowing of cattle would be heard, or the bleating of lambs responding at the street corners.

Indeed, the cowherds and shepherds had driven their animals there, and they were mooing from time to time, while tearing off with their tongues some scraps of foliage that hung down over their snouts.
Rodolphe had moved closer to Emma, and he was speaking quickly in a low voice:
--Doesn't this conspiracy of the world revolt you?
Is there a single feeling that it does not condemn?
The noblest instincts, the purest sympathies are persecuted, slandered, and if two poor souls finally meet, everything is arranged so that they cannot join together.
They will try, however; they will flap their wings, they will call to each other.
Oh! It doesn't matter; sooner or later, in six months, ten years, they will come together, they will love each other, because fate demands it and they were born for each other.

sentences: However, this last alternative would probably have yielded no satisfactory results.

Indeed, according to the maps, which are quite imperfect, it is true, of this portion of the American coastline, the shore, starting from Cape Bathurst, bending westward, descended below the seventieth parallel, and only crossed it again in that Russian America where the English had no rights to settle.
It was not without reason that Jasper Hobson, after carefully studying the cartography of these northern lands, had headed towards Cape Bathurst.

This cape, in fact, juts out like a point above the seventieth parallel, and, between the hundredth and hundred-fiftieth meridians, no other promontory belonging to the continent proper, that is to say, to English America, extends beyond this circle.
It remained to determine whether Cape Bathurst actually occupied the position assigned to it by the most modern maps.
Such was, in summary, the important question that the precise observations of Thomas Black and Jasper Hobson were about to resolve.
The sun was approaching, at that moment, the highest point of its course.
The two observers then aimed the telescope of their sextant at the celestial body that was still rising.

By means of the inclined mirrors arranged on the instrument, the sun was supposed to be, apparently, brought down to the very horizon, and the moment when it would seem to touch the horizon by the lower edge of its disk would be precisely the moment when it reached the highest point of the daily arc, and, consequently, the exact moment when it would cross the meridian, that is to say, noon at that location.
Everyone was watching and maintained a deep silence.
"Noon!" Jasper Hobson soon exclaimed.
-- It's noon!" replied Thomas Black at that very moment.
The glasses were immediately lowered.
The lieutenant and the astronomer read the values of the angles they had just obtained on the graduated limbs and immediately began to calculate their observations.
A few minutes later, Lieutenant Hobson stood up and, addressing his companions:
"My friends," he said to them, "starting from today, July 6th, the Hudson's Bay Company, committing by my word, is doubling the salary that has been assigned to you!
-- Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah for the Company!" shouted the worthy companions of Lieutenant Hobson in unison.

sentences: We used to throw our caps on the ground when we entered the classroom, so that we would have our hands free afterwards; as soon as we reached the threshold of the door, we had to toss them under the bench, so they would hit the wall and create a lot of dust; that was the way it was.
But whether he hadn't noticed this maneuver or hadn't dared to comply, by the time the prayer was over, the new boy was still holding his cap on his knees.

It was one of those composite hats, where you can find elements of a fur cap, a chapska, a round hat, an otter cap, and a cotton bonnet, one of those poor things, in short, whose silent ugliness has depths of expression like the face of an idiot.

Ovoid and bulging with whalebones, it started with three circular rolls; then, separated by a red band, there alternated diamonds of velvet and rabbit fur; next came a kind of bag that ended in a cardboard polygon, covered with complicated soutache embroidery, from which hung, at the end of a long, too-thin cord, a small cross of golden threads, like a tassel.
It was new; the visor was shining.
“Stand up,” said the teacher.
He stood up; his cap fell.
The whole class started to laugh.
He bent down to pick it up.
A classmate knocked it down with an elbow, and he picked it up once again.
“So get rid of your helmet,” said the teacher, who was a witty man.
There was a loud laugh from the schoolboys that flustered the poor boy, so much so that he didn't know whether to keep his cap in his hand, leave it on the ground, or put it on his head.
He sat back down and placed it on his knees.
Stand up, the teacher said again, and tell me your name.
The newcomer articulated, in a stammering voice, an unintelligible name.
Repeat!
The same jumble of syllables could be heard, drowned out by the jeers of the class.
Louder! shouted the teacher, louder!
The newcomer, then taking an extreme resolution, opened his mouth wide and shouted at the top of his lungs, as if to call someone, this word: Charbovari.
It was a racket that sprang up suddenly, rising in crescendo, with sharp bursts of voices (they were howling, barking, stamping their feet, repeating: Charbovari!

Charbovari!), then it rolled into isolated notes, calming down with great difficulty, and sometimes suddenly picked up again along a bench where, like a poorly extinguished firecracker, some muffled laughter still popped up here and there.

sentences: Sir! Morrel exclaimed, grasping the limp hand of the paralytic, they are asking me who I am and what right I have to be here.
Oh you who know, say it, you! Say it!
And the young man's voice faded into sobs.
As for the old man, his labored breathing shook his chest.
It seemed as if he were caught up in those agitations that precede death.
Finally, tears burst forth from Noirtier's eyes, happier than the young man who sobbed without crying.
His head unable to bend, his eyes closed.
Say, Morrel continued in a choked voice, say that I was her fiancé!
Say that she was my noble friend, my only love on earth!
Say, say, say, that this corpse belongs to me!
And the young man, presenting the terrible sight of great strength breaking, fell heavily to his knees before the bed, which his clenched fingers gripped violently.

This pain was so poignant that d'Avrigny turned away to hide his emotion, and Villefort, without asking for further explanation, drawn by the magnetism that pulls us toward those who loved those we mourn, extended his hand to the young man.
But Morrel saw nothing; he had grasped Valentine’s cold hand, and unable to cry, he bit the sheets while roaring.
For some time, all that could be heard in this room was the clash of sobs, curses, and prayer.
And yet, one sound dominated all of those: it was the hoarse and tearing gasp that seemed, with each intake of breath, to break one of the springs of life in Noirtier's chest.
Finally, Villefort, the most composed of all, after having, so to speak, ceded his place for a time to Maximilien, Villefort spoke up.

"Sir," he said to Maximilien, "you loved Valentine, you say: you were her fiancé; I was unaware of this love, I was unaware of this engagement; and yet, I, her father, forgive you, for I see that your pain is great, real, and true.
"Moreover, my own pain is too great for there to be room in my heart for anger."

"But, as you see, the angel you hoped for has left the earth: she no longer cares for the adoration of men, she who, at this hour, adores the Lord; so bid farewell, sir, to the sad remains she has left behind among us; take her hand one last time, and part from her forever: Valentine no longer needs anything but the priest who is to bless her.
