sentences: When they arrived in front of her garden, Madame Bovary pushed open the little gate, ran up the steps, and disappeared.
Léon went back to the lawyer's office where he worked.
The boss was absent; he took a glance at the files, then sharpened a quill, finally put on his hat, and left.
He went to the Pâture, at the top of the Argueil slope, at the entrance to the forest; he lay down on the ground under the pines and looked at the sky through his fingers.
How bored I am! he kept telling himself, how bored I am!
He found it pitiful to live in this village, with Homais as a friend and Mr. Guillaumin as a master.

The latter, completely preoccupied with business, wearing gold-rimmed glasses and red sideburns on a white cravat, understood nothing of the subtleties of the mind, although he affected a stiff and English style that had dazzled the clerk in the early days.

As for the pharmacist's wife, she was the best wife in Normandy, gentle as a lamb, cherishing her children, her father, her mother, her cousins, crying at the misfortunes of others, letting everything go in her household, and hating corsets; — but so slow to move, so boring to listen to, with such a common appearance and such limited conversation, that he had never thought, although she was thirty years old, that he was twenty, that they lived door to door, and that he spoke to her every day, that she could be a woman for someone, nor that she possessed anything of her sex other than her dress.
And then, what was there?

Binet, a few merchants, two or three innkeepers, the priest, and finally Mr. Tuvache, the mayor, with his two sons, well-off, gruff, dull, cultivating their own land, having family feasts, devout besides, and from a society that was completely unbearable.
But, against the common background of all these human faces, Emma's figure stood out, isolated and yet more distant; for he felt between her and himself like vague abysses.

At the beginning, he had come to her several times in the company of the pharmacist; Charles had not seemed extremely eager to receive him; and Léon did not know how to handle the fear of being indiscreet and the desire for an intimacy that he considered almost impossible.

sentences: I live in the city, on the fourth floor.
My apartment is small.
I don't have a garden, but I have a balcony.
It is small too.
For me, it's a treasure.
On my balcony, there are plants, flowers, a small table, and a chair.
In the morning, I drink my coffee here.
I listen to the birds.
I look at the street below.
In summer, my balcony becomes beautiful.
My flowers are red and yellow.
I water them every evening.
This year, I'm trying something new: growing tomatoes in pots!
My mother says, 'Impossible!'
But my plants are growing well.
I have a visitor: a little gray bird.
He comes almost every morning.
I put seeds on the table.
He eats, looks at me, and leaves.
I call him Gaston.
In the evening, during summer, I eat outside.
The sky turns pink, then dark blue.
My balcony is small.
But happiness doesn't need much space.

sentences: Last Sunday, there was a flea market in my neighborhood.
The main street was closed to cars.
The residents were selling their old items in front of their homes.
I love flea markets: you never know what you will find.
I arrived early, around nine o'clock.
You could find everything: clothes, books, toys, bikes, records.
First, I looked at the books.
A man was selling his entire library.
And then, surprise: I found a book from my childhood, the same one I read when I was ten.
I bought it for one euro.
Further on, a lady was selling an old radio.
"Does it still work?" I asked.
She plugged it in, and the radio turned on with a nice old sound.
I hesitated, but it was a bit too expensive for me.
At the flea market, you have to negotiate.
It's part of the game!
A seller was asking ten euros for an old lamp.
"Five euros?" I offered.
"Eight," he replied.
"Seven, and I'll tell you its story."
Sold!
The lamp came from his grandfather's café.
At noon, I came back with my treasures: the book, the lamp, and a nearly new sweater for two euros.
Tonight, the lamp is on my desk.
A new object has no history.
An old object has a thousand.
That's why I love flea markets.

sentences: During the spring break, my parents announced the day's plan: a visit to a castle by the Loire.
My sister Inès sighed very loudly.
"A castle?
More history?"
Dad smiled: "Wait and see."
The castle appeared at the end of a tree-lined path.
Even Inès said "wow."
Round towers, pointed roofs, white walls reflecting in the river.
Our guide, Mr. Perrin, knew a thousand stories.
In the great hall, he showed us the huge fireplace: "Here, they used to roast a whole beef for the king's celebrations."
Inès was listening, her eyes wide open.
She even asked three questions!
Everyone's favorite moment: the spiral staircase of the big tower.
One hundred thirty-seven steps!
At the top, the view was amazing: the Loire, the vineyards, the small villages.
After the castle, we visited the gardens.
Mom took a hundred photos.
Dad took a nap on a bench, "to admire the castle's sky."
At the shop, Inès bought a book about the castles of the Loire.
Our Inès, who hates history!
In the car, she read the whole way.
That night, dad winked at me.
The story is not boring.
It is poorly told sometimes.
Thank you, Mr. Perrin.

sentences: Between twenty-five and thirty-five years old, my physical activity was basically just running after the bus.
Work, fatigue, and evening series: I always had a great excuse.
I kept telling myself, 'I'll get back to it next month' — and the next months piled up for ten years.
The trigger came from a mundane scene.
While climbing four flights of stairs with my groceries, on the day the elevator was out of order, I arrived out of breath like after a marathon.
At thirty-five, four flights of stairs brought me to my knees.
That evening, I decided to get back to it.
For real.
My first attempt was an instructive disaster.
Full of enthusiasm, I put on my old sneakers and went out to run "like before."
I lasted twelve minutes.
In the following three days, I discovered muscles I didn't even know existed, only because they hurt.
My motivation died with my soreness, and the sneakers went back into the closet for two months.
It's a doctor friend who explained my mistake to me: "You want to make up for ten years in a week.
Your heart is ready to progress quickly, but your tendons and joints need months.
Start ridiculously small."
Ridiculously small.
These words changed everything.
Second attempt, new method: twenty minutes of brisk walking, twice a week.
It was almost too easy — and that was exactly the goal.
It's impossible to find an excuse for twenty minutes.
After a month, I moved on to three sessions alternating between walking and slow running.
Then running gradually replaced walking.
A year later, the results exceeded everything I had hoped for.
I run for forty-five minutes without suffering, three times a week.
I sleep deeply, whereas I used to wake up every night.
My back, which had been bothering me for years from sitting at a desk, has calmed down.
And the four flights of stairs?
I go up them while talking on the phone.
If you find yourself in the same situation I was in, here's what I wish I had heard earlier.
Start smaller than your pride would like.
Aim for consistency, not performance: two sessions completed are better than five sessions imagined.
Expect a dip in motivation around the third week — it will pass.
And find enjoyment in the activity itself; otherwise, you won't last.
The body surprisingly forgives many years of neglect.
It only asks that you return to it with patience.

sentences: Buy now, pay later.
This promise is everywhere: in stores, online, at the end of our online purchases.
Consumer credit has made almost everything immediately accessible, without waiting to save up.
It's convenient, sometimes useful, but it's also a trap that many people fall into.
The principle of credit is simple: a bank or a store lends you money for a purchase, and you pay it back gradually, each month.
The problem is that this money isn't free.
In exchange for the loan, you have to pay interest.
In other words, the item bought on credit ends up costing more — sometimes much more — than its displayed price.
The danger comes from the ease.
Since we don't pay right away, it feels like the expense is small: "only thirty euros a month."
But these small monthly payments add up.
We take out a loan for a sofa, another for a phone, another for a vacation, and soon a large part of our salary goes each month to repayments.
That's how we end up in debt without even realizing it.
Credit isn't bad in itself.
Borrowing can make sense for an important and lasting project, like housing, or in case of a real necessity.
But you should always ask yourself the same question before signing: am I borrowing for a real need, or just because I don't have the patience to save?
The wisest rule can be summed up in one sentence: never go into debt for a fleeting pleasure.
The sofa will be old long before the debt is paid off, and you'll continue to pay for something you don't even enjoy anymore.
In the face of advertising that pushes us to consume right away, the old habit of waiting and saving is often the most profitable — and the most peaceful.

sentences: This winter, it hasn't snowed a single time here.
Not once.
In December, in January, in February: it was gray and damp, with temperatures of eight or ten degrees.
It rained a lot, but the water stayed water.
My children were disappointed.
My daughter asked me, "Are we going to make a snowman this year?"
I replied, "We'll see."
We didn't make one.
This isn't the first time.
Last winter, it snowed only one day, and the snow melted before evening.
One Sunday, we had lunch at my grandmother's.
My daughter talked to her about the snow.
My grandmother smiled, then she told about her childhood in the same village.
Every winter, there was snow for weeks.
My brother and I went to school on skis because the road was closed.
My daughter looked at her with wide eyes.
Skis?
To go to school?
Every winter," my grandmother replied.
Then she added, "Here, snow was normal.
Now, it's an event."
In the car, my daughter was silent.
Then she asked, "Will it snow again when I am grown up?"
I didn't know what to answer.

sentences: One day, I will leave the city.
Many city dwellers say this.
Some really do it.
It's interesting to listen to what they say afterwards.
The reasons for leaving often look similar: the cost of housing, fatigue, noise, the desire for a garden, and sometimes the birth of a child.
The possibility of remote work has made this project realistic for people who, in the past, would not have been able to consider it.
Those who succeed in their move almost always mention the same factors.
First, they chose a place they already knew, where they had family or friends.
Arriving somewhere without knowing anyone is much more difficult than one might think.
Then, they checked the practical aspects before leaving: internet coverage, the distance to school, the doctor, and the supermarket.
These details seem secondary from an apartment in the city; they shape daily life in the countryside.
Finally, they got involved in local life — the sports club, the festival committee, the school.
Those who stick to themselves, without ever participating, often feel isolated after a year.
Those who return to the city mention three things: isolation, dependence on the car for even the smallest trips, and their teenagers' boredom.
So there is no general right answer.
The real question is not 'city or countryside?', but 'what am I fleeing from, and what am I looking for?'.
Those who leave just to escape are rarely satisfied.

sentences: Technology is neutral; it all depends on how we use it.
This phrase, repeated a thousand times, has something reassuring about it: it places the responsibility entirely on the user and absolves the tool itself.
A knife can cut bread or injure; it is not the knife that decides.
The idea seems sensible.
However, upon closer inspection, it is largely insufficient.
Because while all technology allows for multiple uses, it does not allow them all equally.
Each tool makes certain actions easy and others difficult; it inclines, it directs, it suggests.
A car does not force anyone to drive fast, but it makes speed possible and desirable in a way that a bicycle does not.
A social network does not compel anyone to compare themselves to others, but it is designed in such a way that comparison becomes almost inevitable.
The tool does not decide for us, but it is also not indifferent to what we do with it.
We can go further.
Some technologies carry effects within them that go beyond any individual use.
The automobile, by becoming widespread, not only transported people: it reshaped cities, dispersed living spaces, and transformed our ways of life.
No one had decided this; it is the tool itself that, by its own logic, has shaped the world around it.
Claiming that it was 'neutral' is to ignore this power of transformation.
Recognizing this does not mean holding technology responsible for everything, nor absolving individuals.
We remain free in our uses, and this freedom is real.
But it is exercised within a framework that the tool has already, in part, established.
Ignoring this framework is to believe oneself freer than one is, and to become blind to the forces that influence our behaviors.
The issue is important because it concerns how we conceive of technologies themselves.
If we accept that they are not neutral, then it becomes legitimate to ask, even before adopting them, what uses they promote and what effects they produce.
The question is no longer just 'how will I use it?', but 'what will this tool do to me, and to us?'
Believing that technology is neutral means giving up on judging it.
However, the tools we create shape us in return, and it's better to know this before they change us.

sentences: He made it on his own.
This phrase, spoken with admiration, celebrates someone who, starting from nothing, would have built their success solely through their own merits, without owing anything to anyone.
The myth of the self-made man, the man who makes himself, occupies a central place in the imagination of our societies, where it serves as a model and justification.
But this myth, as appealing as it may be, is based on an illusion that needs to be dispelled, as it has significant consequences for how we think about merit, success, and justice.
The illusion is to believe that a success can be entirely the work of the person who experiences it, without owing anything to others or to circumstances.
However, no success is ever purely individual.

The successful person has benefited from countless conditions they did not create: an education received, a language learned, knowledge accumulated by others, institutions that made their activity possible, a society that provided the framework for their success, and people who helped, trained, and supported them.
Even the most self-taught of entrepreneurs has used roads they did not build, knowledge they did not invent, and a social order they did not establish.
No one truly makes it on their own; every success is supported by a multitude of invisible contributions.
In addition, there is a considerable and often denied element of luck.

Those who succeed owe a lot to favorable circumstances for which they are not responsible: being born with certain talents, in a certain environment, at a certain time, meeting the right people, seizing the right opportunities, and escaping the misfortunes that have shattered other paths.
This element of luck is completely erased by the myth of the self-made man, which attributes solely to merit what is largely due to chance.
Yet for every person who has succeeded thanks to their efforts and luck, how many have made the same efforts without experiencing the same fortune, lacking the same favorable circumstances?
Why is this myth so persistent, despite its obvious fragility?
Because it is flattering and reassuring, both for those who have succeeded and for the social order.

For those who have succeeded, it is gratifying to attribute their success to their own merit, rather than to acknowledge what they owe to others and to luck; this justifies enjoying the full fruits of their success, without any debt to anyone.

For the social order, the myth justifies inequalities: if everyone is the architect of their own fate, then the rich deserve their wealth and the poor deserve their poverty, and the existing order is just.
Thus, the myth of the self-made man is an ideology that legitimizes inequalities by presenting them as the rightful reflection of merit.
Dispel this myth has significant consequences.
Recognizing that no success is purely individual, that it owes a lot to others, to society, to chance, is to acknowledge a debt.
Those who have succeeded have not only rights over what they have acquired; they also have obligations to this society and to those others without whom they could have achieved nothing.
Success is not a right that one has fully earned, but a shared fruit that calls for a contribution in return.
It is undermining the myth of the self-made man that allows us to establish the idea that those who have received the most must also give the most back.
It is not about denying all merit, pretending that efforts and qualities count for nothing, that everything is just chance and circumstances.
Indeed, those who succeed have often worked, persevered, and demonstrated real qualities, and it would be unjust to deny that.
It is about rejecting the opposite illusion, the one that attributes everything to the individual alone, forgetting all that has supported them.
The truth lies between the two: success combines merit, the contributions of others, and chance, and honesty consists of recognizing all three.
"I made it on my own" is a lie, not because the one who says it has done nothing, but because they forget everything without which what they have done would have been useless.

sentences: Once the first page was turned, she let me browse through it at my leisure; and I flipped through so many chapters that our candles burned down completely.

Then, after thanking her, I was making my way back to my room quietly when a rough hand stopped me; and a voice, that of Rivet, whispered in my ear: "Haven't you finished sorting out the matter of that pig Morin yet?"
From seven o'clock in the morning, she personally brought me a cup of chocolate.
I've never had any like it.
A chocolate to die for, rich, velvety, fragrant, intoxicating.
I couldn't take my mouth away from the delicious rim of her cup.
Hardly had the young girl left when Rivet entered.
He seemed a bit nervous, irritated like a man who hasn't slept much, and he said to me in a grumpy tone: "If you keep this up, you know, you'll end up ruining the matter of that pig Morin."
At eight o'clock, my aunt arrived.
The discussion was brief.
The good people withdrew their complaint, and I would leave five hundred francs to the poor of the area.
So they wanted to keep us to spend the day.
They would even organize an outing to visit some ruins.
Henriette, behind her parents' backs, was nodding at me: "Yes, do stay."
I agreed, but Rivet was determined to leave.

sentences: Mr. Aronnax, replied the Canadian, your arguments are fundamentally flawed.
You speak in the future: "We will be there!
We will be here!"
I speak in the present: "We are here, and we must take advantage of it."
I was closely pressed by Ned Land's logic, and I felt defeated on this ground.
I no longer knew what arguments to present in my favor.
"Sir, Ned continued, let's suppose, for the sake of argument, that Captain Nemo offers you freedom today.
Will you accept?
-- I don't know, I replied.
-- And if he adds that this offer he is making you today, he will not renew it later, will you accept?"
I did not respond.
And what does our friend Conseil think? asked Ned Land.
-- Our friend Conseil, this worthy young man replied calmly, has nothing to say.
He is completely uninterested in the matter.
Like his master and his companion Ned, he is single.
Neither a wife, nor parents, nor children are waiting for him back home.
He is in the service of sir, he thinks like sir, he speaks like sir, and, much to his regret, he cannot be counted on to form a majority.
Only two people are present: sir on one side, Ned Land on the other.
That said, our friend Conseil listens, and he is ready to take note.

sentences: I took her hand, a bit confused, stammering: "Sorry, sorry, miss.
I hurt you; I was brutal!
Don't hold it against me.
If you only knew?..."
I was vainly looking for an excuse.
She said, after a moment: "I have nothing to know, sir."
But I had found it; I exclaimed: "Miss, I have loved you for a year!"
She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued: "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I couldn't care less about him.
I don't care if he goes to prison and to court.
I saw you here last year; you were over there, by the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you, and your image has never left me.
Believe me or don't believe me, I don't care.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized the pretext of that fool Morin; and here I am.
Circumstances have pushed me beyond limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me."
She was watching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured: "Joker."
I raised my hand, and, in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): "I swear to you that I am not lying."
She simply said: "Come on."
We were all alone, just Rivet and I, with the uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made her a true declaration, long and sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to make of it.
I eventually started to feel troubled; reflecting on what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, shivering; and gently, I took her waist.

sentences: But what catches the eye the most is, in front of the Lion d'Or inn, Mr. Homais' pharmacy!

In the evening, especially when his lamp is lit and the red and green jars that adorn his storefront cast their two colored lights far onto the ground; then, through them, like in Bengal fires, the shadow of the pharmacist can be seen, leaning on his desk.

His house, from top to bottom, is covered with inscriptions written in English, in round letters, in molded letters: "Vichy, Seltz and Barèges waters, purgative remedies, Raspail medicine, Arab racahout, Darcet pastilles, Regnault paste, bandages, baths, health chocolates, etc."
And the sign, which spans the entire width of the shop, displays in gold letters: Homais, pharmacist.

Then, at the back of the shop, behind the large scales fixed to the counter, the word laboratory unfolds above a glass door that, halfway up, repeats once again Homais, in gold letters, on a black background.
There is nothing more to see in Yonville.
The street (the only one), a gunshot long and lined with a few shops, ends abruptly at the bend in the road.
If you keep it on the right and follow the bottom of the Saint-Jean hill, you soon arrive at the cemetery.

During the cholera outbreak, to expand it, a section of wall was torn down and three acres of land were purchased next to it; but this new portion is almost uninhabited, with the graves, as before, continuing to pile up towards the gate.
The caretaker, who is also the gravedigger and church beadle (thus deriving a double benefit from the parish corpses), has taken advantage of the empty land to plant potatoes.
Year after year, however, his small field shrinks, and when an epidemic occurs, he doesn't know whether to rejoice at the deaths or mourn the burials.
— You feed on the dead, Lestiboudois! said Mr. Curé to him one day.
These dark words made him think; they stopped him for a while; but even today, he continues to cultivate his tubers and even confidently claims that they grow naturally.
